title: The mobile visit for a manufacturer
metaTitle: The mobile visit to a manufacturer site
excerpt: On a phone, the first screen still has to show the object, how it is made, and a way to reach sales or a spec. The desktop layout should not decide that screen.
alt: An OPEN sign hanging in a shop window, with the word SHOP printed on the glass, for a piece on a first screen a buyer can read at a glance.
caption: A shop window that says what it is immediately. A phone screen should be that plain. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What has to fit on a manufacturer's first phone screen?
faqs.answer: The object, one line about how it is made, and the action. If any of those sit below a tall hero, the hero is too tall. Write the short headline first, then give the wide screen more air around the same words.

faqs.question: How should a spec work on a phone?
faqs.answer: The full drawing can remain a PDF. The page should also carry a short summary of materials, sizes, finishes, and what is custom, in text a person can read without pinch-zoom. Say the file size before a large download on a weak connection.

faqs.question: When should the phone layout be reviewed?
faqs.answer: Before the wide layout is approved. Run a script on a phone in your hand: name the object, open the spec, find sales, and repeat from a proof link. Defects like a table that overflows are layout defects, not a later phase.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
A manufacturer mobile website is where a lot of serious buyers will make the first judgment. On a phone, the first screen still has to show the object, how it is made, and a way to talk to sales or download a spec. A buyer who needs specs and confidence will not wait through a desktop composition that only reveals the offer after a tall hero. Design the phone page as the page.

Do this even if your team reviews work on a laptop. The forwarded link, the search result opened in a hallway, and the tab beside a photo of a drawing are normal visits. If those visits cannot see the part and the next step, the wide layout is a private draft that happens to be public.

## The first screen, at a narrow width

Set the width to a phone and read the top of the homepage without scrolling. You should see the object, a line that says what it is, a line or a compact sequence about how it is made, and the action. If any of those four sit below the first screen, move them up. The desktop arrangement can be solved second.

The headline has to fit without becoming a puzzle of line breaks. A long slogan that looked elegant on a wide measure will hyphenate into nonsense on a narrow one. Write the short version first. The object, the buyer, the offer. Then allow the wide screen more air, more image, and the same words.

The photograph crops in. A wide environmental frame often loses the part at the edge, or shrinks it under a headline. Use the vertical select from the shoot, the one where the object occupies the center. Give it a height that leaves room for the action. A full-viewport image with the button underneath is a desktop habit. On a phone it spends the first screen on atmosphere.

Nielsen Norman Group's research on [how long people stay on web pages](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) is especially sharp here. People often leave in the first 10–20 seconds, and they are still likely to leave through the following moments unless the page has already shown its value. On a phone there is less room to spend those seconds on a roof, a lobby, or a slogan. Spend them on the part.

## Specs that can be used in one hand

A spec download has to be a file a person can open on the phone and actually read. A multi-column drawing that requires pinch-zoom gymnastics will be saved for later and often lost. Provide the file, and also provide a short HTML summary of the facts a buyer checks first: materials, size range, finishes, what is standard, what is custom, the revision. The PDF can carry the full drawing. The page can carry the decision.

Make the download obvious and honest about size. A buyer on a plant floor connection should know they are fetching a document, not a hidden video. If you gate the file, the gate has to be short, and the confirmation has to be readable on the same screen. A gate that asks for ten fields will be abandoned. Ask for what you need to send the file, and no more.

Tables are the usual break. Wide comparison tables overflow, or they shrink until the numbers are decoration. Stack the comparison, or show one product at a time, or turn the critical rows into sentences. The buyer needs a few comparisons, not a miniature spreadsheet. Test with a real spec, not with placeholder prices that happen to be short.

Process sequences should stack. Four steps in a horizontal line become four unreadable fragments on a phone. A vertical list with a plain verb in each step keeps the "how it is made" promise. You can still use a single process photograph above the list. The list is what they will remember and forward.

## The action, where a thumb can reach it

Place the primary action where it can be tapped without covering it with a hand, and keep it available as the reader moves. A header control that stays visible, "Spec" or "Sales," solves the case where the first screen is understood and the reader wants to act from further down. The control should use the same verb as the button in the page.

Give the control space. A tiny text link crowded against the logo will be missed and mis-tapped. The [W3C's WCAG overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) describes operable content as content people can use, not only look at. On this site that means the path to sales or a spec is a real control, with a visible name, with room around it, and with a destination that works on the same phone.

Forms that start the sales path should show the right keyboard and a label that stays visible. Email, a short note about the part, a way to attach a drawing if that is truly the first step. If attachments are awkward on mobile, say that a link to a file is welcome, or offer the spec download as the path that does not require an upload. Do not force a desktop ritual onto a phone and then wonder why inquiries drop.

Tap-to-call and tap-to-email are useful when a person answers. Publish a number that reaches the sales desk during the hours you keep. A number that lands in a general voicemail the buyer did not ask for is a broken action. If the real path is a form or a spec, do not add a phone number to look available.

## Speed and stability on an ordinary connection

The product image is likely the largest element on the screen. web.dev's [Web Vitals](https://web.dev/articles/vitals) separate three problems a buyer feels immediately. Largest Contentful Paint is about when the main content appears. Interaction to Next Paint is about whether taps respond. Cumulative Layout Shift is about whether the page jumps while it loads. A late, heavy hero, a button that moves when the image arrives, and a menu that lags are all mobile failures of a manufacturer site.

Reserve space for the image. Compress the phone crop specifically. It can be a smaller file than the desktop crop. Do not load a background video, a third-party font parade, and a chat widget before the part is visible. Each of those delays the only content that earns the next ten seconds.

Test on a phone you did not buy this year, on a connection that is merely fine. Office wifi hides sins. A buyer walking between buildings will not be on your office wifi. Look at the homepage, a service block, a proof, and the spec summary. If any of them shift as they settle, fix the dimensions. If any of them take long enough that you reach for the desktop out of impatience, the file is too heavy or the page is doing too much.

Motion should be optional and quiet. A slow fade that delays the headline is a cost. People who set their device to reduce motion should get the object and the action at once. The craft standard is the same as on a careful marketing site Hanabi would ship: the movement may support the part, and it may never block the part.

## Pages that tend to break first

Proof pages break when the images are wide, the captions are long, and the next step is a desktop-only button at the end. Keep the constraint in the first lines, the object image in a vertical crop, and the action repeated. A buyer who felt the story was relevant should be able to reach sales without a precision scroll.

Pricing pages break when the shape of the price is trapped in a wide table. Lead with the sentences: how you quote, what is included, what is not, the minimum. Let a table follow only if it still makes sense stacked. The decision to talk or to download has to stay in reach while they read the exclusions.

About pages break when a founder portrait becomes a full-screen intro and the accountability, who quotes, who checks, sits three swipes down. Put the names and the roles up high. The portrait can be smaller. The buyer is there to see who stands behind the offer, and they are holding a small screen.

Navigation breaks when the action lives inside the menu and the menu is closed by default. Keep spec or sales visible in the header. Use the same labels as the wide site. Check that the open menu can be closed, that focus is visible if someone uses a keyboard or a switch, and that the logo returns home. These are basic. They are also the things that get dropped when a desktop nav is merely collapsed by a theme.

## Review the phone before you approve the wide screen

Make the review a script, and run it on a phone in your hand. From the homepage, name the object out loud. Say how it is made, in one sentence. Download the spec or open the summary. Find sales. Open a proof from a direct link and repeat. If you have to turn the phone sideways to understand a drawing, note it as a defect in the page, even if the PDF itself is a drawing.

Do this with someone from sales, because they know which facts buyers ask for while standing somewhere inconvenient. They will notice a missing minimum, a missing material, a form that cannot accept the file type customers send. Design review that only checks alignment on a laptop will approve a site the buyer's phone has already rejected.

Write the defects as layout defects, not as content for later. "Hero too tall," "spec table overflows," "action only in the footer." Fix them in the same pass as the visual design. A punch list that says "mobile later" is how the desktop composition quietly wins.

When you want the phone visit treated as the brief, look at [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). The studio designs and builds the site, and the narrow screen is part of the craft, alongside type, speed, and a repository you can keep. Bring the page you have and open it on your phone in the meeting. The first screen will settle the argument faster than a slide.

Once the small screen can carry the offer, the remaining leak is what happens when a buyer is ready to talk. [A contact path for a manufacturer](/blog/a-contact-path-for-a-manufacturer) is the next piece, because the form, the reply, and the list of what to have ready are where a convinced buyer is most often lost.
